Ἄκουε, φησί, τὸ πονηρὸν ἐγκρατεύου καὶ μὴ ποίει αὐτό· τὸ δὲ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ἐγκρατεύου, ἀλλὰ ποίει αὐτό. ἐὰν γὰρ ἐγκρατεύσῃ τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ποιεῖν, ἁμαρτίαν μεγάλην ἐργάζῃ· ἐὰν δὲ ἐγκρατεύσῃ τὸ πονηρὸν μὴ ποιεῖν, δικαιοσύνην μεγάλην ἐργάζῃ. ἐγκράτευσαι οὖν ἀπὸ πονηρίας πάσης ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθόν. 3 Ποταπαί, φημί, κύριε, εἰσὶν αἱ πονηρίαι, ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἡμᾶς δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι; Ἄκουε, φησίν· ἀπὸ μοιχείας καὶ πορνείας, ἀπὸ μεθύσματος ἀνομίας, ἀπὸ τρυφῆς πονηρᾶς, ἀπό ἐδεσμάτων πολλῶν καὶ πολυτελείας πλούτου καὶ καυχήσεως καὶ ὑψηλοφροσύνης καὶ ὑπερηφανίας καὶ ἀπὸ ψεύσματος καὶ καταλαλιᾶς καὶ ὑποκρίσεως, μνησικακίας καὶ πάσης βλασφημίας. 4 ταῦτα τὰ ἔργα πάντων πονηρότατά εἰσιν ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἀπὸ τούτων οὖν τῶν ἔργων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ θεοῦ· ὁ γὰρ μὴ ἐγκρατευόμενος ἀπὸ τούτων οὐ δύναται ζῆσαι τῷ θεῷ. ἄκουε οὖν καὶ τὰ ἀκόλουθα τούτων, 5. Ἔτι γάρ, φημί, κύριε, πονηρὰ ἔργα ἐστί; καί γε πολλά, φησίν, ἔστιν, ἀφ᾿ ὧν δεῖ τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι· κλέμμα, ψεῦδος, ἀποστέρησις, ψευδομαρτυρία, πλεονεξία, ἐπιθυμία πονηρά, ἀπάτη, κενοδοξία, ἀλαζονεία καὶ ὅσα τούτοις ὅμοιά εἰσιν. 6 οὐ δοκεῖ σοί ταῦτα πονηρὰ εἶναι; καὶ λίαν πονηρά, φημί, τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ. τούτων πάντων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν δουλεύοντα τῷ θεῷ. ἐγκράτευσαι οὖν ἀπὸ πάντων τούτων, ἵνα ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐγγραφήσῃ μετὰ τῶν ἐγκρατευομένων αὐτά. ὧν μὲν οὖν δεῖ σὲ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, ταῦτά ἐστιν. 7 ἃ δὲ δεῖ σὲ μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, φησίν, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖν, ἄκουε. τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ἐγκρατεύου, ἀλλὰ ποίει αὐτό. 8 Καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν μοι, φημί, κύριε, δήλωσον τὴν δύναμιν, ἵνα πορευθῶ ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ δουλεύσω αὐτοῖς, ἵνα ἐργασάμενος αὐτὰ δυνηθῶ σωθῆναι. Ἄκουε, φησί, καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὰ ἔργα, ἅ σὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι. 9 πρῶτον πάντων πίστις, φόβος κυρίου, ἀγάπη, ὁμόνοια, ῥήματα δικαιοσύνης, ἀλήθεια, ὑπομονή· τούτων ἀγαθώτερον οὐδέν ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ταῦτα ἐὰν τις φυλάσσῃ καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύηται ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, μακάριος γίνεται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ. 10 εἶτα τούτων τὰ ἀκόλουθα ἄκουσον· χήραις ὑπηρετεῖν, ὀρφανοὺς καὶ ὑστερουμένους ἐπισκέπτεσθαι, ἐξ ἀναγκῶν λυτροῦσθαι τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ, φιλόξενον εἶναι (ἐν γὰρ τῇ φιλοξενίᾳ εὑρίσκεται ἀγαθοποίησίς ποτε), μηδενὶ ἀντιτάσσεσθαι, ἡσύχιον εἶναι, ἐνδεέστερον γίνεσθαι πάντων ἀνθρώπων, πρεσβύτας σέβεσθαι, δικαιοσύνην ἀσκεῖν, ἀδελφότητα συντηρεῖν, ὕβριν ὑποφέρειν, μακρόθυμον εἶναι, μνησικακίαν μὴ ἔχειν, κάμνοντας τῇ ψυχῇ παρακαλεῖν, ἐσκανδαλισμένους ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως μὴ ἀποβάλλεσθαι, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπιστρέφειν καὶ εὐθύμους ποιεῖν, ἁμαρτάνοντας νουθετεῖν, χρεώστας μὴ θλίβειν καὶ ἐνδεεῖς, καὶ εἴ τινα τούτοις ὅμοιά ἐστι. 11 δοκεῖ σοι, φησί, ταῦτα ἀγαθὰ εἶναι; Τί γάρ, φημί, κύριε, τούτων ἀγαθώτερον; Πορεύου οὖν, φησίν, ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύου ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ· 12 φύλασσε οὖν τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην· ἐὰν τὸ ἀγαθὸν ποιῇς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύσῃ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ οἱ οὕτω ποιοῦντες. καὶ πάλιν ἐὰν τὸ πονηρὸν μὴ ποιῇς καὶ ἐγκρατεύσῃ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ, ὅσοι ἐὰν ταύτας τὰς ἐντολὰς φυλάξωσι καὶ πορευθῶσιν ἐν αὐταῖς.

translation.text:
“I said to you,” he says[1], “that the things created by God are twofold; for self‑control is twofold as well. For with regard to some things one must exercise self‑control, and with regard to others one must not.

“Make it known to me, Lord,” I say, “with respect to what things one must exercise self‑control, and with respect to what things one must not.” “Listen,” he says: “Exercise self‑control with regard to what is evil and do not do it; but do not exercise self‑control with regard to what is good—rather, do it. For if you exercise self‑control so as not to do the good, you commit a great sin; but if you exercise self‑control so as not to do what is evil, you accomplish great righteousness. Therefore exercise self‑control from every wickedness, doing the good.”

“What kinds, Lord,” I say, “are the wickednesses from which we must exercise self‑control?” “Listen,” he says: “From adultery and fornication, from lawless drunkenness,[2] from wicked luxury, from many foods[3] and the extravagance of wealth and boasting and haughtiness and arrogance, and from lying and slander and hypocrisy, resentment, and every blasphemy.

“These deeds are the most evil of all in the life of human beings. From these works[2], then, the servant of God must exercise self‑control; for the one who does not exercise self‑control from these is not able to live to God.[4] Listen, then, also to the things that follow these.”

“Are there still,” I say, “Lord, evil works?” “Indeed, there are many,” he says, “from which the servant of God must exercise self‑control: theft, falsehood, defrauding, false testimony, greed, evil desire, deceit, vainglory, boastful pretension, and whatever things are like these.”

“Do these not seem to you to be evil?” “Very evil,” I say, “for the servants of God.” “From all these the one who serves God must exercise self‑control. Exercise self‑control, then, from all these, that you may live to God and be enrolled[5] with those who exercise self‑control from them. These, then, are the things from which you must exercise self‑control.

“But the things from which you must not exercise self‑control,” he says, “but rather do them—listen: Do not exercise self‑control with regard to the good, but do it.”

“And of the good things, Lord,” I say, “declare to me their power, so that I may walk in them and serve them, that by practicing them I may be able to be saved.” “Listen,” he says, “also to the works of the good, which you must do and not exercise self‑control from.

“First of all: faith, fear of the Lord, love, concord, words of righteousness,[6] truth, endurance—there is nothing better than these in the life of human beings. If someone keeps these and does not exercise self‑control from them, he becomes blessed in his life.

“Next, hear what follows these: to serve widows; to visit orphans and those in want; to redeem the servants of God from distresses;[7] to be hospitable (for in hospitality one sometimes finds an opportunity for doing good[12]); to oppose no one; to be quiet;[8] to make yourself one who has less than all people;[9] to honor the elderly; to practice righteousness; to preserve the brotherhood; to endure insult; to be long‑suffering; to have no resentment; to encourage those who are weary in soul; not to cast off those who have scandalized away from the faith,[10] but to turn them back and make them cheerful; to admonish those who sin; not to press debtors and the needy;[11] and if there is anything like these.

“Do these seem to you to be good?” “What, Lord, is better than these?” I say. “Go, then,” he says, “walk in them and do not exercise self‑control from them, and you will live to God.

“Therefore keep this commandment. If you do the good and do not exercise self‑control from it, you will live to God—and all who act in this way will live to God. And again, if you do not do the evil and exercise self‑control from it, you will live to God[12][11][10][9][8][7][6][5][4][3]; and all will live to God—whoever keeps these commandments and walks in them.”

footnotes.text: “Twofold” signals Hermas’s recurring motif of paired ways (evil/good; restrain/do). The phrase “things created by God are twofold” introduces the moral polarity that follows.
μεθύσμα ἀνομίας: a binge or bout of drinking characterized by lawless excess; hence “lawless drunkenness.”
ἐδέσματα πολλὰ: literally “many foods/dishes,” pointing to excess in eating (delicacies).
“Live to God” is Hermas’s preferred idiom for a life oriented toward God. It echoes early Christian diction and is kept intentionally.
“Be enrolled” evokes civic registers or a record; Hermas does not specify which book, but the image is of being listed among the self‑restrained.
ῥήματα δικαιοσύνης could be rendered “righteous speech” or “just words.” The literal “words of righteousness” is retained.
ἐξ ἀναγκῶν λυτροῦσθαι: literally “to ransom from necessities/constraints,” i.e., to rescue fellow believers from pressing hardships, debts, or bondage.
ἐνδεέστερον γίνεσθαι πάντων ἀνθρώπων: literally “to become more in want than all people,” i.e., willingly accept lack so as to prefer others.
“Scandalized away from the faith” reflects the verb σκανδαλίζω; alternatives include “stumbled” or “led astray.”
“Not to press debtors” (χρεώστας μὴ θλίβειν) has the sense of not dunning or harassing those who owe, especially the needy.
“Doing good” renders ἀγαθοποίησις—beneficence; hospitality often provides concrete opportunities for such good works.

lexical_decisions.rationale: κτίσμα denotes what is created; “things created” avoids limiting the sense to living creatures and suits Hermas’s generic moral framing.
As a noun, ἐγκράτεια is best as “self-control.” The verb emphasizes active restraint; “hold back” keeps the rhetorical contrast with doing the good.
In this moral catalog context, “evil” and “wickedness” preserve the ethical weight without colloquial weakening.
Hermas contrasts “the evil” and “the good.” The definite form keeps the symmetry and weight.
The dative with ζάω here matches idiomatic early-Christian phrasing. Retaining “to God” preserves Hermas’s distinctive diction and teleology.
Project doctrine favors “slave” where the bonded relationship is salient. Hermas stresses belonging to God and obedience, so “slave” carries the intended force.
μεθύσμα is a bout of drinking; with ἀνομίας it connotes unrestrained, unlawful excess. “Lawless drunkenness” is concise and faithful.
τρυφή is luxury/soft living; modifying with πονηρά marks morally corrupt indulgence.
Literal “many foods” preserves the concrete image of excess at table; a footnote clarifies the nuance of abundance/delicacies.
πολυτέλεια is costly display; “extravagance” captures conspicuous expense tied to wealth.
Standard moral-catalog gloss retaining forensic and social harm nuances.
Captures the sense of harboring ill will and not letting go of past wrongs.
Concrete legal/moral term; “theft” is the standard noun form.
Refers to wrongful deprivation of what is owed; “defrauding” fits well in vice lists.
Traditional rendering that preserves the nuance of glorying in emptiness; fits Hermas’s moral tone.
Conveys boastful swagger and false claims; paired with vainglory to avoid redundancy with “pride.”
“Concord” is concise and preserves the sense of shared mind/peace among believers.
Literal rendering retains the concrete focus on speech that accords with righteousness; footnote supplies an idiomatic alternative.
“Endurance” emphasizes active steadfast perseverance, fitting Hermas’s exhortational context.
Ὑπηρετεῖν implies practical service; “serve” is clear and concrete.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to visit orphans (and those in want)
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπισκέπτομαι is to visit with care; “visit” preserves the idiom while implying concern.
λυτρόω has the sense of ransoming; ἀνάγκαι are compulsions/distresses. The chosen rendering keeps the economic-rescue imagery.
Standard Christian virtue term; retains early-church texture without paraphrase.
The abstract noun denotes the practice of beneficence; “doing good” is idiomatic and clear.
“Quiet” matches the moral tone and classical usage of ἡσύχιος as calm, not contentious.

lexical_decisions.chosen: to make yourself one who has less than all people
alternatives: to accept being in want more than others
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐνδεής means lacking/in need; Hermas exhorts voluntary lowliness and self‑limitation for others’ sake. The chosen rendering keeps the literal nuance with a voluntary-reflexive flavor.
πρεσβύτης here denotes age, not office. “Honor the elderly” captures deference to the aged.
“Brotherhood” reflects early Christian familial identity; “preserve” underscores active maintenance.
Here as something to endure; “insult” captures affronts without importing legal nuance.
Traditional rendering that keeps the rich, active sense of enduring provocation.
Literal yet intelligible phrasing that preserves Hermas’s pastoral tone.

alternatives: caused to stumble from the faith
lexical_decisions.rationale: Keeps the distinctive “scandal” idiom and the prepositional nuance of moving away from faith.
εὔθυμος is cheerful/confident; “cheerful” pairs with the preceding pastoral actions.
Technical term for moral admonition, fitting paraenetic register.
θλίβω can mean to press/afflict; in economic context, “press” (i.e., dun) captures the sense.
Civic/record-keeping metaphor; “enrolled” retains the formal image without specifying the book.
Hermas uses ἐντολή as moral mandate; “commandment” preserves weight and traditional moral tone.

translation.text: “What kinds, Lord,” I say, “are the wickednesses from which we must exercise self‑control?” “Listen,” he says: “From adultery and fornication, from lawless drunkenness, from wicked luxury, from many foods and the extravagance of wealth and boasting and haughtiness and arrogance, and from lying and slander and hypocrisy, resentment, and every blasphemy.

translation.text: “Are there still,” I say, “Lord, evil works?” “Indeed, there are many,” he says, “from which the servant of God must exercise self‑control: theft, falsehood, defrauding, false testimony, greed, evil desire, deceit, vainglory, boastfulness, and whatever things are like these.”

translation.text: “Next, hear what follows these: to serve widows; to visit orphans and those in want; to redeem the servants of God from distresses; to be hospitable (for in hospitality one sometimes finds an opportunity for doing good); to oppose no one; to be quiet; to become lower than all people; to honor the elderly; to practice righteousness; to preserve the brotherhood; to endure insult; to be long‑suffering; to have no resentment; to encourage those who are weary in soul; not to cast off those who have stumbled away from the faith, but to turn them back and make them cheerful; to admonish those who sin; not to oppress debtors and the needy; and if there is anything like these.

Ἄκουε, φησί, τὸ πονηρὸν ἐγκρατεύου καὶ μὴ ποίει αὐτό· τὸ δὲ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ἐγκρατεύου, ἀλλὰ ποίει αὐτό. ἐὰν γὰρ ἐγκρατεύσῃ τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ποιεῖν, ἁμαρτίαν μεγάλην ἐργάζῃ· ἐὰν δὲ ἐγκρατεύσῃ τὸ πονηρὸν μὴ ποιεῖν, δικαιοσύνην μεγάλην ἐργάζῃ. ἐγκράτευσαι οὖν ἀπὸ πονηρίας πάσης ἐργαζόμενος τὸ ἀγαθόν. 3 Ποταπαί, φημί, κύριε, εἰσὶν αἱ πονηρίαι, ἀφ᾿ ὧν ἡμᾶς δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι; Ἄκουε, φησίν· ἀπὸ μοιχείας καὶ πορνείας, ἀπὸ μεθύσματος ἀνομίας, ἀπὸ τρυφῆς πονηρᾶς, ἀπό ἐδεσμάτων πολλῶν καὶ πολυτελείας πλούτου καὶ καυχήσεως καὶ ὑψηλοφροσύνης καὶ ὑπερηφανίας καὶ ἀπὸ ψεύσματος καὶ καταλαλιᾶς καὶ ὑποκρίσεως, μνησικακίας καὶ πάσης βλασφημίας. 4 ταῦτα τὰ ἔργα πάντων πονηρότατά εἰσιν ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ἀπὸ τούτων οὖν τῶν ἔργων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ θεοῦ· ὁ γὰρ μὴ ἐγκρατευόμενος ἀπὸ τούτων οὐ δύναται ζῆσαι τῷ θεῷ. ἄκουε οὖν καὶ τὰ ἀκόλουθα τούτων, 5. Ἔτι γάρ, φημί, κύριε, πονηρὰ ἔργα ἐστί; καί γε πολλά, φησίν, ἔστιν, ἀφ᾿ ὧν δεῖ τὸν δοῦλον τοῦ θεοῦ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι· κλέμμα, ψεῦδος, ἀποστέρησις, ψευδομαρτυρία, πλεονεξία, ἐπιθυμία πονηρά, ἀπάτη, κενοδοξία, ἀλαζονεία καὶ ὅσα τούτοις ὅμοιά εἰσιν. 6 οὐ δοκεῖ σοί ταῦτα πονηρὰ εἶναι; καὶ λίαν πονηρά, φημί, τοῖς δούλοις τοῦ θεοῦ. τούτων πάντων δεῖ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι τὸν δουλεύοντα τῷ θεῷ. ἐγκράτευσαι οὖν ἀπὸ πάντων τούτων, ἵνα ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ καὶ ἐγγραφήσῃ μετὰ τῶν ἐγκρατευομένων αὐτά. ὧν μὲν οὖν δεῖ σὲ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, ταῦτά ἐστιν. 7 ἃ δὲ δεῖ σὲ μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι, φησίν, ἀλλὰ ποιεῖν, ἄκουε. τὸ ἀγαθὸν μὴ ἐγκρατεύου, ἀλλὰ ποίει αὐτό. 8 Καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν μοι, φημί, κύριε, δήλωσον τὴν δύναμιν, ἵνα πορευθῶ ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ δουλεύσω αὐτοῖς, ἵνα ἐργασάμενος αὐτὰ δυνηθῶ σωθῆναι. Ἄκουε, φησί, καὶ τῶν ἀγαθῶν τὰ ἔργα, ἅ σὲ δεῖ ἐργάζεσθαι καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύεσθαι. 9 πρῶτον πάντων πίστις, φόβος κυρίου, ἀγάπη, ὁμόνοια, ῥήματα δικαιοσύνης, ἀλήθεια, ὑπομονή· τούτων ἀγαθώτερον οὐδέν ἐστιν ἐν τῇ ζωῇ τῶν ἀνθρώπων. ταῦτα ἐὰν τις φυλάσσῃ καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύηται ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, μακάριος γίνεται ἐν τῇ ζωῇ αὐτοῦ. 10 εἶτα τούτων τὰ ἀκόλουθα ἄκουσον· χήραις ὑπηρετεῖν, ὀρφανοὺς καὶ ὑστερουμένους ἐπισκέπτεσθαι, ἐξ ἀναγκῶν λυτροῦσθαι τοὺς δούλους τοῦ θεοῦ, φιλόξενον εἶναι (ἐν γὰρ τῇ φιλοξενίᾳ εὑρίσκεται ἀγαθοποίησίς ποτε), μηδενὶ ἀντιτάσσεσθαι, ἡσύχιον εἶναι, ἐνδεέστερον γίνεσθαι πάντων ἀνθρώπων, πρεσβύτας σέβεσθαι, δικαιοσύνην ἀσκεῖν, ἀδελφότητα συντηρεῖν, ὕβριν ὑποφέρειν, μακρόθυμον εἶναι, μνησικακίαν μὴ ἔχειν, κάμνοντας τῇ ψυχῇ παρακαλεῖν, ἐσκανδαλισμένους ἀπὸ τῆς πίστεως μὴ ἀποβάλλεσθαι, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπιστρέφειν καὶ εὐθύμους ποιεῖν, ἁμαρτάνοντας νουθετεῖν, χρεώστας μὴ θλίβειν καὶ ἐνδεεῖς, καὶ εἴ τινα τούτοις ὅμοιά ἐστι. 11 δοκεῖ σοι, φησί, ταῦτα ἀγαθὰ εἶναι; Τί γάρ, φημί, κύριε, τούτων ἀγαθώτερον; Πορεύου οὖν, φησίν, ἐν αὐτοῖς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύου ἀπ᾿ αὐτῶν, καὶ ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ· 12 φύλασσε οὖν τὴν ἐντολὴν ταύτην· ἐὰν τὸ ἀγαθὸν ποιῇς καὶ μὴ ἐγκρατεύσῃ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ οἱ οὕτω ποιοῦντες. καὶ πάλιν ἐὰν τὸ πονηρὸν μὴ ποιῇς καὶ ἐγκρατεύσῃ ἀπ᾿ αὐτοῦ, ζήσῃ τῷ θεῷ, καὶ πάντες ζήσονται τῷ θεῷ, ὅσοι ἐὰν ταύτας τὰς ἐντολὰς φυλάξωσι καὶ πορευθῶσιν ἐν αὐταῖς.

translation.text: “Therefore keep this commandment. If you do the good and do not exercise self‑control from it, you will live to God—and all who act in this way will live to God. base_translation.text: “Make it known to me, Lord,” I say, “with respect to what things one must exercise self‑control, and with respect to what things one must not.” “Listen,” he says: “Exercise self‑control with regard to what is evil and do not do it; but do not exercise self‑control with regard to what is good—rather, do it. For if you exercise self‑control so as not to do the good, you commit a great sin; but if you exercise self‑control so as not to do what is evil, you accomplish great righteousness. Therefore exercise self‑control from every wickedness, doing the good.”

base_translation.text: “Do these seem to you to be good?” “What, Lord, is better than these?” I say. “Go, then,” he says, “walk in them and do not exercise self‑control from them, and you will live to God.

translation.text:
“Do these things seem good to you?”

“What could be better than these, Lord?” I replied.

“Then make them your way of life,” he said. “Do not hold yourself back from doing them, and you will live for God.”

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: What, Lord, is better than these? I say.
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: What could be better than these, Lord? I replied.
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The speaker answers that nothing is better than the practices just described.
simplification_decisions.rationale: Natural English word order makes the rhetorical answer clear.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: walk in them
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: make them your way of life
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: He must consistently live according to these good practices.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The wording explains the moral-life image rather than reducing it to literal walking.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: do not exercise self-control from them
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Do not hold yourself back from doing them
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: Self-restraint should not prevent him from practicing what is good.
simplification_decisions.rationale: The difficult construction is recast as a direct command without changing its force.

risk_flags.risk: “Live for God” may sound more purpose-oriented than the POB phrase “live to God.”
risk_flags.mitigation: The rendering keeps God as the defining relation of the promised life while using understandable English.

base_translation.text: “Therefore keep this commandment. If you do the good and do not exercise self‑control from it, you will live to God—and all who act in this way will live to God. And again, if you do not do the evil and exercise self‑control from it, you will live to God; and all will live to God—whoever keeps these commandments and walks in them.”

translation.text: Therefore, keep this commandment: Do what is good, and do not hold back from doing it. Then you will live to God, and so will everyone who acts this way. Do not do what is evil, but keep yourself from it. Then you will live to God. Everyone who keeps these commandments and follows them will live to God.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: do the good and do not exercise self-control from it
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Do what is good, and do not hold back from doing it
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The reader must actively do good rather than restrain the impulse to do it.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB main text and immediate contrast
simplification_decisions.rationale: This makes the unusual positive use of self-control clear while preserving both commands.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: do not do the evil and exercise self-control from it
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: Do not do what is evil, but keep yourself from it
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The reader must avoid evil and restrain oneself from it.
simplification_decisions.reasoning_layer_used: POB main text and parallel clause structure
simplification_decisions.rationale: Common wording preserves both refusing evil and practicing restraint against it.

simplification_decisions.pob_phrase: walks in them
simplification_decisions.simplified_phrase: follows them
simplification_decisions.preserved_meaning: The commandments must guide a person's continuing way of life.
simplification_decisions.rationale: “Follows them” clearly expresses living according to the commandments.

risk_flags.risk: “Live to God” is less familiar than “live for God” in modern English.
risk_flags.mitigation: The POB formula is retained because “for God” could narrow the meaning to service on God's behalf.

spob_revision_history.previous_text: Therefore, keep this commandment: Do what is good, and do not hold back from doing it. Then you will live for God, and so will everyone who acts this way. Do not do what is evil, but keep yourself from it. Then you will live for God. Everyone who keeps these commandments and follows them will live for God.
spob_revision_history.review_summary: The draft gives a warranted and genuinely clearer explanation of the unusual positive command not to restrain oneself from doing good. Its rendering of restraint from evil and of walking in the commandments is also clear and contextually faithful. However, replacing the repeated “live to God” with “live for God” introduces a potentially narrower service-oriented sense. Retain the POB phrase in this publication text; its repeated contextual use makes it understandable enough without adding a doctrinal explanation.
